utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours. Yesterday, in relation to the earlier part of the history generally, the Croatian indictment and part of the Bosnian indictment, I set out the range of links that may be shown connecting this accused to various crimes with which he is charged, and shortly I'm going to return, although I hope in swifter form this morning or in a swifter manner this morning, to those links that exist in relation to the Bosnian indictment. But it may just be useful to pause for a couple of minutes and to take stock of where we are. The Court will remember yesterday in relation to the Croatian indictment - if we could just put that one on the overhead projector again - that I made the point that the declared independent areas that are shown there -- except they're not coming up on my screen at the moment. Are they on Your Honours' screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can proceed without them. But in relation to the declared areas shown there, they would not have been doing what they did simply to achieve independence unless there was something else to be joined to. We pause to observe that if any area such as any one of these, simply fearful of a state it distrusted chose to seek to protect itself, there could be no complaint of that. For example, I suppose, if we look forward, if the Kosovo Albanians, concerned about a state they found threatening, simply protected themselves without any insurgency which might give rise to inquiries by the Office of the Prosecutor, for example, then there could be no complaint about that. But going back to Croatia, it wasn't a case simply of seeking to establish independence, it was absolutely a case of seeking to be joined to something else; namely, to Serbia. And if we just look and remind ourselves that there is a gap between Western Slavonia and Eastern Slavonia, the evidence will probably reveal to the Chamber that there would have been a desire and effort to take that area as well but that it was impossible. But more significantly, what about Eastern Slavonia? Was this an area of Serb population majority? No, it wasn't. The reverse; it was an area where they were in a minority, and yet it was an area that was cleansed. Can we now turn to the map in relation to Bosnia and look at it in just a little bit more detail. My video -- ah, here it is. It's coming up now. The various marks that Your Honours can see surrounded in red or blue indicate the municipalities as declared. The legend at the bottom tells us that. And the Chamber will see that those declared municipalities do not include all the areas to the east that adjoin Serbia, and yet the Chamber will see that it is those eastern areas that were subject to the most, sometimes the most extreme force of ethnic cleansing and violence. In both the case of the eastern parts of Bosnia and the eastern parts of Croatia, when in due course it's possible to analyse from the evidence the degree to which the crimes -- and in our respectful submission, there is going to be no doubt but that the most serious crimes were committed. When one looks to see to what degree the crimes were committed for - committed by the JNA as opposed to being committed by, in the case of Croatia, those who represented the declared municipalities in relation to Bosnia, the army of Republika Srpska - we will find that there was a heavy preponderance of military crime being committed coming from the east, coming from Serbia, whether in the name of the JNA or the VJ or whatever, coming from the east. These --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me see if I've got the point. Eastern Slavonia, you make the point there was not a Serb majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But are you making a similar point in relation to Bosnia or is it a different point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. No, it's the same point but it's even more powerful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which are the areas without the Serb majority?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I take it you -- I'll hand it back. My machine isn't working. If you run down -- if you look at the right-hand side of the map, you'll see that areas of Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica, and Visegrad are not included as the Serbian Autonomous Districts or regions defined by proclamation on the 21st of November. But as you -- and let me explain the map a little more. The areas surrounded in blue or red are, as the legend reveals, the proclaimed Serbian Autonomous Districts. The areas shaded in grey are those that feature in the indictment. So that these areas - Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica, and Visegrad - are not declared on the 21st of November, no Serb majorities, subject of ethnic cleansing and other dreadful crimes, as we've already heard; and the evidence will show in both this case and also again in the case of Croatia that the eastern regions were subject of a high percentage of direct military involvement coming from Eastern Serbia. And the point is perhaps obvious, in our respectful submission, powerful. These regions in both states, Croatia and Bosnia, declaring their autonomy or independence, weren't just doing it for themselves. They were doing it in order to be joined to something else. Was it purely fortuitous that they wanted to be joined to something that was going to be headed by this accused, or was he, as we say, for all the reasons already advanced, a party to precisely that plan? The facts I have just summarised, of course, indicate powerfully that of course he was a party to that plan. We heard yesterday of somebody saying that he would become their leader in the event of joinder. Of course he would. Whether, in the room where things were discussed, it was a question of "Do this" or, "Here's a problem," leaving its resolution to the others tacitly agreed, whether it was a question of others bringing a plan and his approving it matters not, for criminal culpability would always follow. But the events and, of course, his failure ever to stop the events show the culpability there was. We've rather assumed, and perhaps unhelpfully to some of those watching, we've rather assumed that everybody knows the map of Yugoslavia from working in this place. We haven't actually put one on the overhead projector, and perhaps at some stage we ought to do so, although the overhead projector isn't the best vehicle really for seeing maps. But -- if I can move the microphone. For those who are less familiar, what I'm saying is that the areas here are the areas subject of this particular concern by the accused, we would say, and others. The consequence of success in these areas in joining up Slavonia with Western Slavonia, the consequences of success in Bosnia would be, of course, to create an enormous area joined up and going round under Serb control. Your Honour, with that recap of yesterday's position, can I return to where we were, but as I've indicated, having given the accused an opportunity to know the categories of material, the natures of connections upon which we rely, I will now attempt to move more swiftly. We ended yesterday with the listed connections between the army of the Republika Srpska and Serbia itself. It's necessary to mention one or two other personalities, but very briefly. Some of them will recur elsewhere. Jovica Stanisic was a man who was a close associate of this accused, one of his closest. The man responsible for establishing special operations units which became known as the Red Berets. He's a man whom we must have in mind. He's a man who features not only at this early stage but who features significantly in Kosovo when we find, so far as he is concerned, something of a change of mind. He, Stanisic, founder of the Red Berets, had close, very close contacts with this accused. Another man, Frenki Simatovic, referred to as chief of the unit that was initially known as something else and then came to be known as the Red Berets, a man who would often brag to his men of a direct line of communication that he had with this accused through the previously-mentioned Jovica Stanisic. We've got a picture of somebody wearing a red beret. Next we'll just put on that to show what the Red Berets look like. This isn't anybody in particular - it is to him, of course - but it's a Red Beret uniform. The man Simatovic supplied Arkan with ammunition and supplies and had a close relationship with Arkan until 1994, when Arkan's Tigers were incorporated into the ranks of the Red Berets. Further connections and connections to this accused. Simatovic used the Red Berets to help distribute weapons in both Croatia and Bosnia. And putting the Red Berets and Perisic together very briefly, there was a time when Perisic was Commander in Mostar when he initially may have objected to the Red Berets being there because they took orders directly from Belgrade. He was overruled on that eventually. I'm not going to say more about Arkan. I dealt with him at some length yesterday, save to say that on one occasion when Arkan was engaged in training some trainees, he was overheard by a witness who will be before you, to say this: "Those who will not cut throats, kill, maim, and eliminate all those who dare to stand against the Serb state will be killed." And in light of the general conduct of that man, it will be evidenced, it may be thought a genuine rather than -- a genuine protestation rather than mere bravado. I've already dealt briefly with the Serbian Ministry of Defence. I say very little more about it at the moment save to say this; that the accused was instrumental in passing or having passed a Serbian law on defence on the 18th of July of 1991, which placed the police and the Territorial Defence under his personal control. And, and I think we've now got Article 39 of the order that dealt with that. It reads as follows: "In times of war or an immediate threat of war and emergency situations, the Territorial Defence may be reinforced with volunteers too." The significance of that may become apparent a little later. Arkan had dealings with the Ministry of Defence as established by this accused; further connections. The accused himself had very regular contacts with that ministry and daily contact with the man General Simovic, who was its head for a time. The Bosnian MUP, another body of which you'll become aware in the evidence, established early in 1992 when the authority of the republican MUP was abolished. There's another intercept which you'll hear of in due course, or you'll hear in due course, between Karadzic and this accused where Karadzic told the accused this: "The Muslims were simply heading towards division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We will carry out the establishment of regions and set up our MUPs wherever we are in power." It will not be possible, in our submission, for this accused to say that silence is anything less than involved participation when these material and important telephone intercepts become evidence in the case for the MUP played a leading role in the takeover of municipalities and in the persecution of the non-Serb population. Another key to the takeover of Bosnia was the arming of local Serbs, something again that we'll find repeated in Kosovo, showing a constancy of behaviour. Thus, then, several more connections beyond those that I referred to yesterday. As to the crime or crime base, as we refer to it in these trials, in Bosnia it wasn't anything other than a takeover of towns. It was not a conflict, it was a takeover of towns and municipalities. How was it done? Well, maybe a good illustration is to be found in what was said by somebody, a party member from Bosanska Krupa regarding the takeover of that town; a speech or contribution to the 16th Assembly of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, where a Mr. Vjestica made these remarks, informing his audience of the situation in the theatre of war in the municipality of Bosanski Krupa. "What have we done," he said, "in this municipality? I must tell you to remind you that all there is, only 24 per cent are Serbs in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. That is 14.500 of us, and there are 47.000 Muslims. For a year and a half, we have been preparing for the war in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa." So indicating preparation back to the beginning of 1991. "I ask a question now," he went on, "which I have the right to ask: How could it happen that two-thirds of the town were taken in two days of operation? On the right bank of the Una River, there are no more Muslims. In the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, all the enclaves that were Rapusa --" and he lists them -- "we have evacuated them so there will be none there for the duration of war operations. Will they have a place to return to? I think it's unlikely after our President told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una River was the border." Well, how was it possible to take over a municipality when they were outnumbered three to one? Because arms had been distributed to the Serb population; because there had been extensive party leadership in the planning; and of course because of the military action supported from elsewhere that was available to them. Let's turn to Bijeljina. We've seen where it is in the northeast of Bosnia. Sixty per cent Serb, 31 per cent Muslim prior to the conflict, although 70 per cent of Bijeljina town was itself Muslim. So this is in the autonomous region, as declared, of Semberija. One of the first targets, it would appear, of those masterminding this operation, and it was Arkan who made, perhaps, his reputation there. He'd been seen in the town frequently enough, familiarising himself with the streets before the attack, an attack which involved the JNA as well as Arkan's men. The JNA which had helped distribute arms in advance to local Serbs. The JNA which provided no protection for the town when Arkan attacked. It did free some of Arkan's men when they were trapped by Muslims. And when Arkan had finished, the JNA moved in to secure the town. A former policeman from this town will describe seeing Arkan there as well as seeing others, including Mrs. Plavsic and a man called Fikret Abdic. Plavsic and Arkan met on plainly familiar terms, and the witness was given the responsibility of collect bodies. As a former policeman, he had some experience the investigation of crimes, and the corpses scattered around the town had, for the most part, died from gunshot wounds in the mouth, temple, or the back of the head, none of them wearing uniforms, and their number including women and children. Coming down the Drina River and now to one of those places that I referred to earlier, Zvornik. Attacked without any provocation by the JNA, as well as paramilitaries. Shelled from positions within Serbia proper. The subject of the attentions of Arkan as well. Kozluk I don't think we have marked. An entire community of Muslims from there, 1.800 in all, gathered up in the Kozluk settlement of Visegrad, and of course the Court will remember how I described one part of this event as my opening passage to Your Honours' Court. But what was interesting is perhaps the ending of Visegrad shown in part on the photograph on the ELMO. Those moved were forced to sign over their property to local Serb leaders and then board buses for Serbia. What happened to them in Serbia? Well, they were kept in a train yard for several days while they were given Serbian passports. With the Serbian passports, they were then transported over the Serbian border into Hungary and Austria. Whose involvement and what level of authority does that reveal? Bratunac. Again to the east, again not within one of the declared autonomous districts. Sixty-four per cent Muslim, 34 per cent Serb. Again the local Serbs had been armed in advance by the JNA. Indeed, the JNA went further, as they did elsewhere; armed the Serbs and disarmed the others. In late 1991, the JNA started installing artillery weapons and mortars into positions facing the town. I go back to my earlier observations this morning: Is this the justified protection by a community of itself or is it entirely the reverse, as this accused well knows? In April, tanks were deployed on the Serbian side of the river with their cannons facing the town, and the takeover began when the JNA Novi Sad Corps moved in on the 16th of April, together with Arkan's Tigers and two of the other groups to which we've referred, White Eagles and Seselj's men, most of them wearing balaclavas. Well, as I said yesterday, we keep ourselves detached, but it is perhaps worth thinking what it must feel like to be in a town, to face that sort of occupation, with consequences that can have been only too easily forecast by the victims-to-be. On the 9th of May, in the Glogova area of Bratunac, south of Zvornik and along the Drina River, 65 Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat civilians were killed by members of that 1st Novi Sad Corps acting with paramilitaries. Eight thousand people were expelled from the municipality, and in January of 1993, six months after the JNA allegedly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. withdrew from Bratunac, they returned to assist Bosnian Serbs when they were in danger of losing the municipality again. And when they got involved on this occasion, it was with tanks and rocket launchers, companies of specialised troops. General Mandic, of the Yugoslavian army, stated in an interview in Belgrade's daily Politika that the presence was pursuant to a decree of the Republic and the Supreme Council. The Chamber will recall that, of course, the accused was a member of that Council. Visegrad, again as referred to earlier: In the course of that takeover, Muslims gathered from the town and surrounding settlements, systematically searched, told what was coming their way by White Eagles who were controlling the town. Then the awful incident I referred to yesterday where women and children were burned to death. I needn't go into that. In June of the same year, in the same area, execution of non-Serbs, including women and children, who were executed and thrown into the Drina River. Summary executions followed. A witness will be before you at about -- covering this period of time, who overheard Radmila -- Radmilo Bogdanovic, a sometime Serbian Minister of the Interior, arguing with the man Seselj in a hotel in Bratunac about the takeover in Visegrad. This is what was overheard: "We gave you money. We gave you men. We gave you weapons. We gave you freedom to do whatever you want. What else do you want from us?" Seselj replied to that former Serbian Minister that in the coming days the work would be done in all the municipalities along the Drina River. Being given freedom to do whatever you want, should that ever turn out to be some form of excuse, is no excuse at all. It is the clearest revelation of criminal complicity. Prijedor. So well-known that -- to the Chamber, I expect, that I need not mention much about it. Can we just look at the picture, please. In the municipality of Prijedor, hundreds of non-Serb civilians systematically killed in various places. A large number of killings continued in various camps, including Omarska and Keraterm, throughout 1992. Karadzic had given a forewarning of the brutality that was going to characterise the campaign. In an order issued on the 22nd of September, 1991, he said this of his own aspirations and of those whom he led: "Should these just and aspirations of the Serbian people be opposed, have no mercy; an eye for an eye." Is the accused detached from that approach if it's an approach that will be established in evidence? It may be thought not thus far by the things that he's said in the hearings here. Yes, we have a video of Prijedor camp. Just have a look at that, please. It's the Trnopolje camp. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "INTERVIEWER: It was the second camp, Trnopolje, where 2.000 refugees were living. We were not prepared for what we saw and heard there. How long has he been here? Several hundred said that they'd arrived from Omarska that morning or from another detention camp, released to this refugee centre after days, sometimes months, of interrogation. We asked if the allegations of beating in the detention centres were true. "INTERVIEWEE: Can't say much about that. See people are hungry, it's true. I'm not sure if I'm allowed about that. Can you understand me? "INTERVIEWER: Tell us the truth. "INTERVIEWEE: I'm afraid. 250. "INTERVIEWER: Killed? What happened?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A pattern repeated elsewhere frequently, in far worse circumstances and with many deaths, as we shall hear, resulting. Sanski Most. Adjacent to Prijedor and Banja Luka. During the takeover in 1992, a hundred non-Serb men brought to Sanski Most from the Keraterm and Omarska camps in Prijedor and killed, detention centres established, and a place to which Arkan returned as late as 1995, when he had been incorporated into the Red Berets, taking the opportunity to kill many Muslims in different locations. Back to Northern Bosnia and the town of Brcko, critical for its position as part of the corridor along the north, adjacent to Bijeljina. It may not be shown on the map -- yes, there it is. Again, not actually originally declared and, of course, a municipality that's had special status since. A place where there was an execution of Bosnian Muslim males at the Hotel Posavina on the 4th of May. And, of course, where there was a Luka camp presided over, at one stage -- or not presided over, the scene of the killings by a man called Jelisic who gave himself the name of Serbian Adolph. Interestingly enough, in that area and on the 20th of May, 1992, the body of a man called Branislav Filipovic was found, apparently a senior member of a paramilitary group. From his body, a number of documents -- or not from his body but from the clothes he was wearing, a number of documents were recovered. They included written authorisation addressed to the JNA headquarters in Belgrade, authorising him to collect weapons; a document stamped the 13th of May, 1992, with a JNA military postcode from Belgrade; documentation that weapons had been delivered -- documenting that weapons had been delivered to the Brcko garrison; travel records from a JNA vehicle; and also passes from Brcko and also from Semberija, the declared municipality to the east, allowing him freedom of movement. Well, what was he doing there with all those documents in the absence of active involvement by Serbia in what was going on at this area of Brcko? A short reference to what was going on down in the south in Herzegovina and near the Montenegro border: Significant loss of life there in Foca and Djidevo and so on; the notorious KP Dom prison; in Nevesinje, many Muslims killed. Finally, I suppose, in reference to Bosanski Samac and Doboj, two municipalities in the Northern Bosnia semi-autonomous district, names well-known here. In the Crkvina camp in Bosanski Samac, 17 non-Serb detainees killed on the 6th of May, the camp not being closed until 1992; seventeen hundred people expelled; and a number of prisoners from Bosanski Samac flown by helicopter into Serbia to a JNA military base of Batajnica, just outside of Belgrade. Well, a report of the VRS in 1993 discussed the results of the takeover, said this: "It could hardly be simpler. Corridors were secured to link Serbian territories with mother Serbia." Your Honours, our case is, I hope, clear. Can I detach us from the events on the ground to something slightly different? Because it comes at the end of 1992 and can fit before I deal, as I must briefly, with Sarajevo and Srebrenica. It's a document that reflects the view of the Secretary of State Eagleburger of the United States, and it may provide an interesting view -- I'm sorry, it's not within your papers. My mistake. I'll get a copy printed and provide it. I'll read it from the overhead projector to make sure that it's legible. "Secretary of State Eagleburger, on Wednesday -" this is December the 16th, 1992, is the press release - "said that Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and the leader of Bosnian Serbs must answer 'in a court of law, I would hope,' for atrocities committed by military and detention camp commanders in shattered Yugoslavia." It went on to dealing with the question of lifting of the embargo and later said this: "The fact of the matter is that we know that crimes against humanity have occurred, we know when and where they occurred. We know, moreover, which forces committed those crimes, and under whose command they operated." Then later: "In short, Eagleburger said, Milosevic and Radovan Karadzic, leader of the Bosnian Serbs, 'have systematically flouted agreements to which they had solemnly, and yet cynically, given their assent.'" And over the page: "Milosevic, Karadzic, General Ratko Mladic, commander of Bosnian Serb military forces, 'must eventually explain whether and how they sought to ensure, as they must under international law, that their forces complied with international law.'" Well, no doubt the accused will make further reference, as he had, to what was to happen later. Dayton and so on. Well, this Tribunal is only concerned, perhaps tangentially, with the workings of politics. Let there be no doubt, first, this accused was already being identified, well-identified for complicity; but second, and the point of irresistible importance in this case, he was on notice from the highest authority of his duty to comply with international law. It will be for the Chamber to decide in due course whether he took any notice of that warning and others like it at all. Sarajevo. We've already seen, of course, what Karadzic said in his six points about what should happen in Sarajevo. And in response to what was happening in Northern Bosnia, the Bosnian President, Alija Izetbegovic, issued a mobilisation call for the Bosnian Territorial Defence. The Bosnian Serb leadership said they regarded this as an act of war. And I have one picture here of a victim of what was to follow in the awful events of Sarajevo. That declaration of war led to some changes in the joint Presidency, particularly insofar as Plavsic was concerned. The day after that declaration, the 5th of April, 1992, Serb paramilitaries laid siege to their police academy in the southern part of the city. Forces moved down from Vraca hill. And this town or city, a clear and long standing example of integration of ethnic groups and tolerance, a place where Muslims, Serbs, Croats, Yugoslavs, and Jews had co-existed, indeed their places of worship cheek by jowl together in the Old Town were subject to the following, as it may be described: The siege of Sarajevo - for that's what it was popularly known as - was an episode, it may be decided, of such notoriety in the conflict of the former Yugoslavia that we must go back to World War II to find a parallel in European history. Not since then had a professional army conducted a campaign of unrelenting violence against the civilians of a European city so to reduce them to a state of medieval deprivation in which they were in constant fear of death. In the time period of this indictment, nowhere safe for a Sarajevan, not at home, at school, in hospital to be free of indiscriminate attack. The civilians who chose to remain in Sarajevo, about 350.000 of them, deliberately targeted by those forces of the VRS that encircled Sarajevo. Through the actions of snipers, civilians were shot in their homes as they watched television, drank coffee or prayed, shot outside their homes as they crossed the street, cleared rubbish, collected wood for heat, or fetched water, as they rode in buses or on trams. In addition, shelling by the VRS, particularly through the use of mortars specifically designed to kill and maim, targeted civilians that queued to collect water at some of the wells, targeted groups of children playing near residences, schools, hospitals, targeted funeral processions, and, of course most notoriously it may be, crowded marketplaces. We accept that our proof against this accused, certainly at this stage, for complicity in these awful events is via his support for the Republika Srpska and via his support for its army. We do not, of course, exclude the possibility of being able to go further in due course. Srebrenica, the safe area so declared until, on the 11th of July, 1995, troops of the Republika Srpska's VRS army and MUP troops under the command of Mladic and others executed over 6.500 Bosnian Muslim men and boys from the Srebrenica enclave. A picture of a mass grave. And that was carried out over a five-day period by firing squads in the area south of Zvornik that we've been looking at. Bratunac. Fifteen hundred men and boys murdered in Bratunac during this period of time in various villages, 5.000 men and boys murdered in Zvornik. The largest single massacre in Europe since World War II. The one distressing photograph we show, the important point perhaps being what can be found around the man's head. In addition to these matters, we expect -- we intend to lead evidence in support of the indictment of extensive systematic plunder and destruction of private property of those expelled, the intentional destruction of mosques, historical and cultural institutions, churches and other buildings; destruction carefully calculated to ensure that when the conflict ended, those expelled had little, if anything, to which to return. Again, as in the previous indictment, I do not need to relate that which is publicly available in the listing of charges against this accused. As a post script and a further link back to Croatia, this small detail: A witness before you will testify that as a member of the military intelligence, he was aware in 1995 of the accused's intention to stop supporting the Krajina and to allow it to fall back into the control of Croatia. Well, whether his measure of control is exactly as substantial as that, something the Prosecution assert, is, of course, for the Tribunal to establish on all the evidence. But the witness can help us further. He and thousands of other Serb refugees crossed into Serbia. We looked, in 1993, at how this accused was prepared to treat his own people when they did things he didn't like. How was he prepared to treat these people? Did he welcome them back or did he use them for his own purposes? They were prevented from leaving the highway by police officers who funneled the fleeing Serbs down to Croatia where they could affect the Serb populations in areas in a minority; all part of an overall plan. I turn to Kosovo. Can we have the Yugoslavian map up, please. Kosovo's rather a small area, really, and it's being marked by Ms. Graham on the map for us. Under the ICTY Statute -- sorry. If I said they were funneled to Croatia in relation to the previous witness, I should have said to Kosovo. And I'm grateful for that. Under the ICTY Statute covered in this indictment, offences charged include crimes against humanity, deportations, transfers, murders, persecution, and violations of the laws and customs of war, such as murder. I dealt yesterday with the overall statistics for Kosovo. A word about its historical context, and we'll put on another map. Shows Kosovo itself, bordered by Montenegro, Serbia, Albania, and so on, rather better. It was one of the two autonomous provinces of the socialist republic, as I explained yesterday, had its own Constitution, local government, and police under that 1994 Constitution, and right up until 1989. It's been tested territory for much of its history, various claims made about people's ancestors and so on. It remained Ottoman or Turkish by rule until 1912 when it was taken by Serbian and Montenegrin forces in the Balkan wars, then to be occupied by the Austro-Hungarians in 1915. Serb troops returned in 1918 and Kosovo became part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. In the Second World War, it was again occupied by Bulgaria, Germany and Italy, and at the end of the Second World War it was formally annexed to Serbia. It's an area that's always been ethnically mixed, containing, of course, Kosovo Albanians and Serbs but also many other groups, including Turks, Roma, and some Croats, and some Bosniaks, and so on. I played yesterday the -- or had played yesterday the Kosovo Polje "No one should dare to beat you" video clip and also the 28th of June, 1989 speech. Between 1989 and 1992, with its autonomy dismantled by Serbia and with its provincial institutions being dissolved, it was effectively being taken over by the Republic of Serbia, and Kosovo Albanians found themselves dismissed from their institutions and jobs and businesses, the majority of them state or socially owned. Discriminatory measures were put in place, it may be thought clearly aimed at altering the ethnic balance in Kosovo; the Serbs were able to come and take jobs, even when they were not particularly qualified for them, getting housing and benefits to lure them there. And indeed, there were the Serb refugees sent there, as I eventually when correctly -- when corrected, reminded you. I think we last picked up the history, and I'm going to deal with the history as briefly as I can, but I must deal with Kosovo in some detail. We picked up the history, I think, with the 7th of September 1990 declaration by the Assembly, the Kosovo Assembly of the Republic of Kosovo. There was then, in 1991, an unofficial referendum where they voted overwhelmingly for independence from Serbia. And in May 1992, they held unofficial elections for an Assembly and a President of what they called the Republic of Kosovo, a parallel government whose dominant political attitude was non-violent resistance. You heard yesterday, of course, of how not so very many years earlier and following the death of Tito, there'd been the cry of Republika Kosovo. That was something that had actually been heard before but we're concerned with its occurrence here and in the relevant part of the history that will drive conclusions in this case. In the face of this legal, social, and economic Serbianisation of Kosovo, the Serbian Assembly denounced its Albanianisation of Kosovo and denounced that as the greatest ethnic cleansing in Europe, carried out, it was said, with the goal of cutting Kosovo off from Serbia and Yugoslavia, arguing at that time, in 1992, that there were many illegal immigrants from Albania inhabiting Kosovo. How detached was it to take this view? How detached from reality was it to take this view when ethnic cleansing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by Serbs was going on in Eastern Bosnia? Well, we pass through those awful conflicts and come, of course, to Dayton in 1995. The effectively non-violent Kosovo Albanians were disappointed in Dayton. Some -- and I said how detached we must be in this Tribunal from the world of politics. Some may have thought that, by Dayton, some aspects of ethnic cleansing had been rewarded. That may have affected the view that those Kosovo Albanians would hold as to the future utility of a non-violent approach. As we look at what was to come and the Dayton peace negotiations, of which no doubt the accused will speak, it's worth reminding ourselves - I needn't list them - that although President of Serbia and not until much later President of Yugoslavia, it was this accused who the politicians turned to between 1991 and 1995. The reason, it may be, as I suggested yesterday, because he did have the power and it was hoped that he was the person who was going to be able to deliver. It may be that he was the person who impressed international negotiators with charm or even seeming reasonableness and moderation, even if appearances were different from what was revealed on the ground. I think he told Your Honours at his initial appearance he should be given credit for peace in Bosnia and not for war. Well, it may be that by the time of Dayton he didn't want war any more, at least not at that time, because peace meant securing for Bosnian Serbs about half of the country that they had devastated. It would mean an end to sanctions that were then in place and it would, of course, end the massive drain of the Bosnian war machine. The Chamber may remember my suggestion yesterday that the first two battles are battles he could afford to win, at least afford for a time until he could go no further. The last one was one he could not afford to lose. But of course, whatever decisions the accused made in 1995 have no effect on his involvement in what was done before if the evidence reveals those to have been crimes. I've already made the point about Secretary of State Eagleburger's view some years earlier. I move on from Dayton because I'm concerned with its effect on the Kosovo Albanians and on the history of what was happening in Kosovo, save of course simply to say this: It would always have been possible, after Dayton, for this accused to have reflected the position he's already represented as being his to this Chamber and to bring to justice men such as Sljivancanin, Mrksic, Mladic, and Arkan if he was sincere. You judge a man, of course, sometimes for his sincerity not by what he says but by what he does. Those men he gave a home and refuge in Serbia, rewarding some of them with promotions and the access to great wealth. Following Dayton, in September 1996, there was an agreement signed by the accused and Ibrahim Rugova, the leader of the Kosovo Albanians, an agreement that should have provided some of the educational rights that had been taken away from the Albanians. Some hoped, actually, that the agreement would be implemented, but it wasn't. But Rugova pursued the non-violence strategy, even though he may have been having little success and getting little for it. So it was in the mid-1990s that a faction of Kosovo Albanians organised a group that we know as the KLA, Kosovo Liberation Army, or UCK in the language of the Kosovo Albanians. And this group advocated a campaign of armed insurgency and violent resistance to the Serbian authorities, and indeed in 1996, mid-1996, started launching attacks primarily on Serbian police forces to which the Serbian police responded forcefully against suspected KLA bases and against suspected supporters of the KLA in Kosovo. In 1996, back in Serbia, or in Serbia generally, the accused may have felt himself under some pressure when local elections did not go his way. This probably followed economic pressures or may have reflected some entente between opposition parties. In any event, it led to the accused having some difficulties between November 1996 and January 1997 with demonstrations against him and so on. The Serbian MUP was pressed to use force against demonstrators. The man Stanisic, to whom I've already referred, resisted. Perisic also signalled he was against the use of the army, and it may be that it's at this time that we will see the beginnings of a rift between these two men and the accused. If so, was he beginning to feel vulnerable? If so, does that perhaps explain some of his subsequent conduct? Although the Chamber will be concerned to establish particular events and particular states of mind by hard evidence, it will inevitably from time to time hear or become acquainted with views about the motivation and driving forces of this accused, and it may be that at some stage it will need to consider as a possibility that this was an accused, a man who, when things were difficult, could find an advantage in, for example, the chaos of war from which he would be subsequently, he hoped, able to rebuild something and move on. Well, if he was facing difficulties at home of one kind or another and even the beginnings of dissent from those upon whom he had to rely, was he reaching the stage where, as I suggested yesterday, the forecast that Kosovo's turn would come was becoming an inevitability? In June of 1997, in speech in Kosovo, the accused made it quite plain that there was to be no international mediation for Kosovo, that it was forever an integral part of Serbia. Milosevic was elected as President of what was called the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the 15th of July of 1997, taking up office on the 23rd of July. And we have another wiring diagram. Now, this is slightly different from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got this? We should have it, if not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the new bundle that you're going on to, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the new bundle that was given yesterday, and I hope it's towards of middle of that, I think. Oh, the third item. Thank you. This is headed differently from the other two because, of course, everything that happens in Kosovo definitely happens within Serbia. It's headed, "De jure command, Yugoslav army, Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs." The top right-hand dotted line box represents the Supreme Defence Council. We've heard of that before. I'm so sorry if people haven't had these. The accused, along with the presidents Djukanovic and Milutinovic, respectively of Montenegro and Serbia, constituted the Supreme Defence Council, and the precise functioning of this council will be a matter of evidence but what it may come to is this; that the President, commanding the army both in war and peace, acted pursuant to decisions made by the council. How that took effect, of course, will depend on the individuals and their true independence or otherwise of the accused, but in any event, he remains - and he told us about this himself - Commander-in-Chief. And we can see that, therefore, he had command of the General Staff, Colonel General Ojdanic, the 3rd Army Colonel General Pavkovic, and then down through them we come to the Pristina Corps and the Pristina military district. Underneath the Supreme Defence Council but not connected to it on this diagram is the President of Serbia, Milutinovic, with a connection, and again a matter for evidence how direct, to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Stojiljkovic, and the MUP. From there, a number of divisions, some of them simply fighting units. And if we come down on the left-hand side through the State Security Division under Markovic, the Special Operations Unit, JSO, under Simatovic was a fighting unit. If we come down on the right-hand side under the Public Security Division of the RDB, Djordjevic, the secretariats of internal affairs, the special police units and the special anti-terrorist units, SUP, PJP, and SAJ, all fighting units. The Prosecution's case is that whatever the technical division under law may have been, in fact the accused had influence on all these bodies, and it may well be effective control. But in any event, under the law on defence, as commander of the army, he had the advantage of control over all units in time of imminent threat of war or a state of war because there was then subordination of the MUP to the VJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you concede that your diagram shows his authority as being confined to specific units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not conceding that his practical authority was confined in any way. This is what the de jure position was in time of peace. In time of war, the subordination of the MUP to the VJ, in any event, so that he would have complete control at that time, and the evidence may well reveal that he had effective control at all times of all units in any event, but this is a diagram to take us forward in looking at the legal position when we have it before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we'll await the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly. This is the legal position. And it's in very short form. I hope, really, a useful way for the Chamber to start its approach to matters of fact and law that it will have to analyse or may have to analyse. So in his position as President, thus in part his powers. In 1987, August, student demonstrations at Pristina. In September 1987 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1997. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Yes, of course, 1997. September, the position didn't improve and there was further armed activity by Kosovo Albanians. In October 1997, the police breaking up non-violent student demonstrations in Pristina. In October of 1997, we have the following apparently sincere dialogue being opened up by the DB with representatives of Kosovo Albanians. But further student demonstrations. And in November, as we will hear from the very first witness in this case, an approach made to leaders of the Kosovo Albanians by those on behalf of the Serbian government where the possibility of Kosovo attaining republic status within the federal Yugoslavia was raised. The Belgrade side of this discussion, if we can so characterise it, rejected that possibility out of hand, saying that if the Albanians insisted on such a demand it meant war. It was also explained at that meeting, as we will hear from the witness, that there was a plan, a "scorched earth" plan that could be implemented within 24 hours to destroy Albanian villages. And the witness was told that the accused and the man Jovica Stanisic knew about the meeting that was being conducted at that time, that it was a meeting with authority. A second such meeting occurred in December of 1997. On this occasion, the witness, from whom we will hear, and Stanisic spoke privately, Stanisic saying that there was a nationalist circle around this accused that would go to war before accepting as a possibility a Kosovo republic. January 1998. The Chamber will, of course, remember that the indictment for Kosovo doesn't start until 1999, but nevertheless, a little of the background of 1998 must be sketched in. In February, the conflict intensified between the KLA and the forces of the Republic of Serbia. A number of Kosovo Albanians and Kosovo Serbs were killed and wounded during this time. The forces of the republic engaged sometimes in shelling Albanian towns and villages, destroying property and expelling populations from areas in which the KLA was or was thought to be active. And indeed the United Nations estimate was that by mid-October of 1998, over 298.000 persons, about 15 per cent of the population, had been internally displaced within Kosovo or had been forced out of the province by what was happening. As early as March of 1998, the Security Council, in its Resolution 1160, condemned the use of excessive force by Serbian police forces against civilians and peaceful demonstrators in Kosovo and imposed an arms embargo on the republic. Six months later, a further Resolution, 1119, was passed, which said that the deterioration of the situation in Kosovo constituted a threat to peace and security in the region and demanded that all parties cease hostility and that the security forces used for civilian repression be withdrawn. It's pretty clear that as a result of what was happening the armed insurgency was enjoying wider sympathy that had formerly been the case and demonstrations supportive of an independent Kosovo, frequently large demonstrations, took place. A mention of a man we've heard before, Vojislav Seselj. In March of this year, 1998, he became the Deputy Prime Minister of Yugoslavia. He, the Chamber will remember, President of the Serbian Radical Party, founder of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, and a Deputy Prime Minister of Serbia from this date until 2000 throughout the period of the war in Kosovo. An outspoken advocate, I remind the Chamber, of the Greater Serbia plan and an express approver of the notion of the ethnic cleansing of the Kosovo. Within Kosovo in 1998, there was one particular attack on the family of Ahmeti in a compound in Likosan [phoen] or Likosane. Sixteen people killed. Ten more killed on the following day. I use the word "compound." There's one feature of Kosovo Albanian life that distinguishes them from others. They live in, for the most part, I think, multi-generational homes, many families or families, extended families, in the same location, and their properties are surrounded by substantial walls that make, quite genuinely and simply, compounds. So when we use the word "compound," it's that we'll be describing. I don't think we have a picture of a typical Kosovo Albanian residence. We will probably find one during the course of the trial. It's a singular feature of the place. Between February 1998 and March of 1998, Perisic and Stanisic suggested to this accused that he should conclude a deal with the leader Rugova, but at the same time special MUP and anti-terrorist units were being sent into Kosovo to deal with the KLA. It was at about this time that the accused was heard to say or said that the actual number of Kosovo Albanians was around 800.000. Does the Chamber remember yesterday how I explained that because of a boycott of the 1991 census estimates only are available of the true population of Kosovo by groups at the material time? Because of that, you will have evidence of demographers and so on to help you. But it may be that there will be little doubt, in due course, but that the figures are radically different from what was being suggested by the accused, this low figure of 800.000. Why did he say things like that? Why did he seek to persuade, if that's what he was doing, that the population was as small, so far as the Albanians were concerned, as he said? Was it because that's what he was hoping would come about or was it in order to make less terrible the presumption he was to take of trying to move the enormous population that in due course he did try to move? The point that he made to the witness I've referred to already was something he made to others. And the Court may wonder whether there was emerging in his mind an exit strategy, as it were, for Kosovo along the lines of the exit strategy that had worked, in a sense, for Bosnia. By the Dayton Agreement, the Serb part of Bosnia, as it had been, was still almost wholly monoethnic in favour of the Serbs. He may have thought, this accused, that blame had been forgotten. He may have thought that whereas the decade of enticing Serbs to Kosovo, luring them there, had not achieved the objective he had in mind that he could do again what he'd done before and not be blamed for it. Your Honour, I don't know if that's a convenient moment or if that's too early.
