utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in 1998, ahead of the indictment period, of course, you will hear of a heavy attack on a compound of the Jashari family where 54 people were killed. It's probably quite clear that there were KLA members or a member or even criminals involved in that compound. The excessive use of force, however, the death of women and children, couldn't be justified or excused. We have a picture of the building. It doesn't actually show the compound nature of the building very well. And then, after that, we have a picture of those people who were killed there, some of them, after they'd been laid out. Next we have, or we will have, a letter or reference to a letter sent by Perisic to the accused from a witness who was protected but whose name has now been revealed to the accused, so he knows where it comes from, explaining that his strategy in Kosovo was to produce casualties, destroy villages and would lead to rebellion. It will be for the Chamber to decide whether the account of this letter is accurate. In April of 1998, the MUP and the VJ were bombarding buildings in the location of Decani. The suggestion is they were ordered from the top, despite the recommendation of the local commander for a surgical intervention, to behave in the way they did. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The first witness to be called before us in a day or so's time met the accused again in April of 1998. The accused spoke of terrorists he was willing to annihilate. There was some negotiation about the position of the Kosovo Albanians. The witness told the accused that what was happening in this fight against terrorism involved attacks on innocent civilians, women and children. So he was on notice, if he had no earlier notice - we say of course he did - of what was being involved. In May of 1998, a group of five Kosovo Albanians met with the accused and his chef de cabinet. They discussed that attack on the Jashari compound, saying it was a case of police brutality. Interestingly enough, the accused - and this may make further relevance to this incident - seemed very well-infomed as to that particular incident. He said it was under investigation, said he had many problems. "I have many nationalists around me," he said, "but we'll solve those problems," and claimed to have full control of Kosovo. We have evidence that there was the arming of the Serbian population of Kosovo in preparation of what was to come. And there's a document - I don't think we're going to produce it at the moment, unless I'm mistaken - going to show quite clearly that weapons were to be distributed to Serbians and the Montenegrin population. In the spring or summer of 1998, there were heavy-handed offensives against the KLA with the shelling of villages, paramilitary shock troops being used, and there was, in June of 1998, the beginning of some attacks on the village of Racak which features, of course, in the history of Kosovo. It may be that there were KLA present there and that that explained why Racak in particular was targeted. In June of 1998, I have some exhibits. I have a document, an order of the 125th Motorised Brigade, a ban on operations without the knowledge and approval of the joint command. We can see that. The joint command thus identified, and the document is dated the 7th of July, comes into existence. Pursuant to the order of the joint command, strictly confidential, number so-and-so, is the aim of increasing effectiveness in performing assignments and so on. Incidentally, I'm sorry that it's always impossible to go into all these documents at length in an opening. To do that, the opening would become far too long. But both was to documents and as to things like speeches, what will matter in due course is the context in which particular passages are placed by the Chamber when it has the document or the exhibit as a whole. But back to the joint command or the joint headquarters, including, as we will discover, apart from the accused, Milutinovic and others, including Pavkovic, Lukic, Sainovic, Stanisic and others. Was this creation of the joint command a turning point and was it something that was going to lead to the events of 1999? Was it a means, the joint command, involving all these people, of circumventing any resistance to the will of this accused or to smooth the way to what was to be unlawful use of the army? Witnesses will speak of that before you. One witness told the accused that the MUP was engaged in operations - this is in the summer of 1998 - against the civilian population. The accused denied it, said the only target was the KLA. But -- and indeed he would continue to insist on that as his explanation. Several witnesses will deal with that in due course and I needn't go into that in any more detail. On the 28th of July of 1998, Peter Ilic, head of the Pristina Defence Administration, issued to all Kosovo municipalities, the joint command for Kosovo, regulations for the defence of inhabited areas including the separation of populations and the use of force by the army, including artillery, support for the MUP, and so on. So plans were in hand at that stage, including separation of the population, including use of the army, to deal with points to come under the joint command for Kosovo. And I move on, trying to save time. On the 24th of June of 1998, still, of course, before the indictment period, a captain Srdjan Perovic from the Pec MUP secretariat reported that during an operation called Thunder, conducted in May and June, platoons of the 24th detachment of a special police unit called the PJP had been subordinated to a body called the JSO which was the body of Frenki's Boys, Frenki being a person we've heard of before. Further recurring connections. The same Captain Perovic also reports flatly that, during the operation, no one "demolished, torched or looted facilities." Why, one might ask, was it necessary to put such a thing in a report? In July of 1998, heavy army and MUP assault on Dulje, Blace, near Junik or in Junik, 30.000 Albanians fled. At the same time, at widely spaced out places in the province of Kosovo, similar things were happening. Suggestive, it may be, even at that stage of coordinated action. Meanwhile, the arming of Serb civilians continued. We'll hear a great deal of detail about that. And there was distribution of weapons in Mitrovica. Some 7.400 weapons distributed to reserve police members in Kosovska Mitrovica SUP area, which was several municipalities. I'm going too fast. Thank you, and I apologise. In August of 1998, the Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission and other diplomats found themselves involved. The army and the MUP often denied freedom of movement to these international monitors and observers, saying that they were denying them movement for their own safety. Therefore, those observers were only ever able to verify shellings or excesses after the event and/or from a distance. Nevertheless, the Chamber may be left in no doubt from them that there were joint army and MUP operations and the use of heavy artillery and tanks against villages at this early stage, or comparatively early stage. Paramilitaries presence was also confirmed, for example, in Dubrava Prison and in a place called Istok. Dubrava Prison, a very large prison in the north-west or thereabouts, north-west centre of the province, is going to feature in the crime base evidence that you'll hear in due course. There was looting and burning going on, again attributed to the MUP and to their special forces, the PJP, in the summer. The accused, when told of these things, denied that there were any such activities, denied that there was fleeing of the police. And when told that there were Albanians crossing the border, he said that they were just fabricating a story for some reason. By the summer of 1998, 200.000 Kosovo Albanians had been expelled. They were astray within Kosovo. They found refugee status, as it were, in the towns and villages that were still under government control, huge numbers staying in the open without shelter, for example, in areas held by the KLA and so on. You'll hear about these displacements and dispersions of individuals. Where there was looting, and there was looting from time to time in excesses against Kosovo Albanians, no intervention by the -- or no satisfactory intervention by the MUP on their behalf. In September of 1998, in Golubovac, some 14 Kosovo Albanians lined up and shot, it may be that the Chamber will be satisfied by MUP special forces. In September of 1998, on the 28th of September, the Serbian Prime Minister, Mirko Marjanovic, publicly stated that government forces had regained unchallenged control of most of Kosovo and that the rebellion of the KLA had largely failed. Peace had returned to Kosovo, he said. However, of course, contemporaneous documents and other evidence reveals to the contrary. And it reveals that the army, the territorial army, was mobilising, that the MUP was calling up reserves, that there was a vigorous effort that was creating tensions with the army reserve mechanisms as both bodies were calling up the same people. The Serbs were being armed, training was being provided, and peace had not returned to Kosovo. On the 29th of September of 1998, Paddy Ashdown told this accused that his troops were violating the Geneva Conventions, and his exchange will be of value to you, that witness having particular experience of his own of relevance. This led to the negotiations between US Ambassador Holbrooke and the accused, involving NATO Generals Naumann and Clark. It's well known, of course, that General Clark has detailed these events in his book, and we'll be hearing from General Naumann, I trust. But statements about Albanians by Milosevic it may be could be characterised of dehumanisation of another group. Straight incitement to ethnic cleansing. And General Naumann will further testify as to the conduct of these negotiations, including that the accused's control appeared to be not only of the VJ, of the army, but of the MUP as well, for whom he appeared to speak. He will also speak of the role of that Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic over both the army and the MUP. In October of 1998, Stanisic was replaced by Markovic as head of the state security of the Serbian MUP, one of several replacements of key positions of the army and the MUP that the Chamber may be satisfied were driven by the accused's need to remove voices of dissent to his policies in Kosovo. A more forceful role for the army with the MUP in Kosovo may have been required than that which the previous office-holders would have approved of. In the area of international politics, the accused was going through the motions of political settlement. Domestically, he was gathering around him persons who, as one witness will explain, were prepared for a brutal resolution of the Kosovo question. Still the documents tell the same story; ethnic division, ethnic mobilisation of one part of society, disarming another. We will hear further how the accused spoke at one stage of knowing how to deal with the Albanians, that in a way that they'd been dealt with in 1946. Albanians who he described as murderers and bandits, saying that they could be killed although it would take -- how they had been handled in 1946. "It had taken several years to kill them but we killed them all." Some such quotation. Not quite clear what it refers to, but in 1946, there was a counter-insurgency in Kosovo, it appears, where there was much destruction of Kosovo Albanian communities and villages. And agree -- a component of the agreement between Holbrooke and Milosevic was the agreement on the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission, signed on the 16th of October by chairman of the OSCE Geremek and the Foreign Affairs Minister Jovanovic for the Republic. This agreement, together with an agreement between General Clark and General Naumann signed by Sainovic and the MUP general, Djordjevic, together with a further agreement between KDOM and MUP, provided for the partial withdrawal of forces of the FRY and Serbia from Kosovo, and also provided that there should be a limitation on additional forces and equipment into the area with the deployment of unarmed OSCE verifiers. At that stage, what was the presence of police in Kosovo? Very considerable. And I will have a look at a picture of the police in due course quite shortly. In October of 1998, 14.500 uniformed police in Kosovo, plus additional 2.000 on leave, some 4.500 of these police were from outside Kosovo already. The numbers included special anti-terrorist units. Ambassador -- the KVM mission included meetings where Milosevic was told that -- I beg your pardon, where Milosevic explained that Albanians were indeed less than 50 per cent of the population. I've dealt with the potential significance of this type of observation before. In October 1998, Perisic stated privately that the situation in Kosovo was the result of one man's action. At a meeting in October 1998, that same General Peresic, normally of a hard tone, was softened when he was able to have a private conversation and able to explain that it was obvious that NATO, if they wanted to, could destroy the army which he wanted to save, saying it was the only democratic institution left in Yugoslavia. He was not prepared for the army to be used for the type of operation that may have been in mind for it. He made it clear that it was the accused who had the authority to decide on agreement and no one else. Tanks and artillery continued, however, to be used or to -- I beg your pardon. At further meetings it was made quite clear to the Serbian leadership that tanks and artillery in use against civilians and villages was not acceptable and that if that wasn't accepted so far as the Serbians were concerned, then NATO would act. The accused rejected all allegations made, claiming that Serb forces were acting in accordance with the law. On one view, it may be - and I've referred already to theories that the Chamber may have to countenance and weigh - the accused was getting exactly what he wanted; a war from which he could pick up the pieces and move on. If this was his recurring strategy, then - and this was a meeting that we'll hear was characterised by his nerves, by nervousness rather than by his nerves - if he was nervous, then perhaps it was because he knew he was about to take a risk, a risk with the lives of other people, which he may not have regarded as highly as the risk that he was taking in his own -- in respect of his own career. But in any event, he rejected the suggestions made, rejected the reality of NATO intervention. That joint command we referred to earlier features again in a report on the 16th of October where it was said that there was a danger of extremist Albanians importing cameras through the offices of the OSCE in order, it said, to provide documentary evidence of alleged crimes and the excess use of violence and repression by state organs against Albanian civilians. Those writing that report were more concerned with the reporting of excesses than the fact that excesses had occurred. We then come to a meeting on the 24th and 25th of October involving Naumann, the accused, and others where he was told that the hammer was cocked and he was told of the shelling of villages by artillery. The accused asked Perisic, who was still there, who denied it, although that same Perisic privately appealed to others to try and settle with the accused. The accused appeared to agree in principle, saying that he had to negotiate further with others, but he then changed any indication of agreement and never signed the agreement that it was open to him at that stage to sign. So that by October, the accused had control of the army, the Federal Ministry of Defence, he had de facto control of the MUP. He designated Sainovic, the federal Deputy Prime Minister and a long-time ally as his representative in Kosovo, and he'd strengthened that position by coordinating the MUP or having coordinated the MUP, the VJ, local defence, Civil Defence, and other institutions on the ground by order of the joint command headed by Sainovic. Serbs and Montenegrins were being armed. Operations of the MUP and the VJ were continuing. A senior official of this very time was still able to see one of the villages, a village called Makrmal, on fire immediately after an attack by the MUP. The question in relation to such events always arises: If this was just an attack on the KLA, why destroy a whole village? The process of disarming the Kosovo Albanians continued, and we have evidence of how they were forced to surrender their weapons. In November, General Dimitrijevic told a witness called Crossland, a military attache, that Perisic was visiting the army in Kosovo, telling them not to react to provocations but that a man called Pavkovic might act outside of the army command, and if he did so, it would be on the orders of this accused via Sainovic. He admitted, indeed, that the army had overstepped the mark that summer. In November it was that the accused finally made the critical replacements of key senior staff. Chief of Staff Perisic was replaced by General Ojdanic. Closely linked was the replacement of General Samardzic by General Pavkovic as the commander of the 3rd Army, and the subsequent elevation of General Lazarevic to fill the post of commander of the Pristina Corps left vacant by Pavkovic's promotion. And what we're looking at is a picture of General Ojdanic. Compliant commanders in Ojdanic and Pavkovic would be needed if this accused was to -- was fully to engage the army and the MUP from the attacks in Kosovo. Ojdanic had been seen, interestingly, at rallies of that party that was associated with the accused's wife. Pavkovic was present at SPS functions, the party of this accused both before and after the war of 1999. In November, the KVM deployed monitors in implementation of the agreement between Holbrooke and the accused but violence continued. As to the man Sainovic, he took an active role in negotiations involving the OSCE, he participated in numerous other meetings, he acted as the accused's liaison to Kosovo Albanians, he exercised control over numerous individuals. He is a man of importance in the story that will unfold. A snapshot: Late 1998 or early 1999, when told that a MUP officer had been seen driving away with a trailer full of looted goods and that other MUP officers were burning a village with gasoline, the accused became agitated. He said this was unacceptable. He took responsibility. He ordered somebody to have the unit that was said to have committed these offences moved. An interesting reaction, but it may not be an uncommon one. Much worse things were to come in Kosovo. Did he take responsibility then? More significant, why just move the unit? Why not, consistent with his duties, investigate, punish, and prevent recurrence? January 1999: Scores of OSCE verifiers throughout Kosovo observe the continuation of hostilities. During this period, verifiers documented Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a number of killings of Kosovo Albanians, the most famous or notorious being Racak. Small, a very small community, quite remote from the village or town to which it is connected. One road in or one small road in, possibly one small road out, a further road out. What happened there in Racak in the municipality of Stimlje was that it was shelled and the fleeing villagers were shot. Twenty-five men found in a building were moved to a nearby hill and shot. Forty, in total, were killed. I said already it was clear that the KLA had been present in Racak. It is also clear that there had been a killing of a policeman, perhaps arguably by the KLA, for which this may have been a revenge attack. The attack doesn't feature in the allegations reflected in the indictment, nevertheless, it will be investigated, perhaps in the evidence, for it had an important effect on what was to follow, and it may be the Chamber will be quite satisfied this was a wholly unjustified attack of the worst kind. Yes. This is an acknowledgement in a document of the 15th of January, 1999, from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia. It says this: "Overview of occurrences and developments and activities: Starting at 0300 hours on the 15th of January, measures were taken to seal off the village of Racak with a view to capturing and destroying a terrorist group which, according to our information, had committed several terrorist attacks with lethal consequences in the territory of Urosevac SUP. At 0630 the village was completely encircled." You've cut out the light. "About --" and then a number is illegible -- "members of the Albanian terrorists were liquidated." And it goes on, materially, "No civilians were hurt during the execution of the operation." Inaccurate and untrue. Intentionally so? A matter for the Chamber to decide. Here are some of the pictures that reflect what was in due course found. A member of the MUP secretariat told a witness that he had indeed been responsible for the attack on Racak, as that document, in a sense we've looked at, would confirm. Shortly after Racak, the accused told a senior policy witness that investigations would show that, "Our people didn't do this." He seemed to have a knowledge of the outcome before any investigation had done to the same -- had been done. He said to the same witness, "Kosovo is more important than my head." General Naumann will explain how, on the 18th of January of 1999, the accused was confident he could solve the Kosovo problem by military means and in a short period of time. Milosevic had been told by now by countless people and through many channels that the means he was using in Kosovo were criminal, were resulting in widespread suffering amongst the civilian population. His own staff were telling him he was generating recruits for the KLA and weakening the moderate voices among Kosovo Albanians. He spoke of using military means. Did he have any other approach in mind or was he simply anticipating the final resolution that was to come? There was a third meeting between Naumann and others and this accused on the 19th of January concerning Racak in particular. He was given a list of incidents in which disproportionate force had been used. He said he'd look into it. On the 29th of January, 12 people were killed in the area of Rugova Djakovica. And we move on to February. Sainovic, along with the President of Serbia, Milutinovic, were involved in the negotiations at Rambouillet. Putting it very shortly, evidence may satisfy the Chamber that while the world was holding its breath, there was a lack of sincerity in these negotiations and that, in any event, those in Rambouillet didn't have the authority without reference back to negotiate. Some witnesses believe that some of those present on the Serb side were trying conscientiously and that will all have to be taken into account, as will the fact that Albanians were perhaps hesitant to sign. The chamber will, if it decides this is an important matter to investigate, will have to see things from all sides. The Prosecution's invitation will be that there was a lack of sincerity. While the peace negotiations were going on, the violence continued and Serbia launched a series of offensives against many or several Kosovo Albanian villages and towns. Coming forward and on the 10th of March, the accused stated he knew that if he hadn't signed in October, he could have cleared up the problem in a week, meaning, no doubt, the KLA problem. He rejected comparisons he was invited to make at that stage with Vietnam or Afghanistan, saying of himself he knew how things should be done, he knew how to do it. On the 20th of March, the party majority on the Serb Assembly rejected what was described as the Paris accord. The situation in Kosovo was unchanged and that throughout the Rambouillet and Paris processes, forces of the FRY and Serbia were massing on the borders. No one will contest that Yugoslavia had a legitimate interest to defend itself against an impending NATO air campaign. No one would contest that of course it had a legitimate interest in preparing for combat against any armed insurgency on its territory. But the accused had been told all that he had been told and had said in reply that he had the intention to provide a definitive resolution. And this was a resolution to use his military. He couldn't help perhaps revealing his obsession with the demographic balance. The Serbian population in Kosovo had been mobilised, as it were, on his behalf and the majority Albanians disarmed. May it be that the NATO campaign he brought upon himself provided him with the opportunity to accomplish those goals while purporting to defend his country. One participant at Rambouillet, a member of the Serbian delegation, was heard to say that if NATO falls, there will be a massacre in Kosovo. Will be. They weren't, of course, the accused's words nor were they true, in a sense, for the massacre effectively came before. Even if there was no devious plan of the kind I summarise, as many think, to lure external violence on Kosovo to justify pushing the Albanians out, the doing of it when it happened is without excuse or justification of any kind and would remain offences as described in this indictment. Agreement was impossible, and in consequence and as a result, the orange vehicles, the KVM monitors, pulled out of Kosovo; the NATO bombs, as we know, began to fall. As they did so and even before, the forces of FRY and Serbia began their systematic attacks against the Albanian population of which we will hear in sufficient detail to equip the Chamber by Mr. Ryneveld in due course. At that stage, there was other evidence of the accused being uninterested, apparently, in further discussion. And on the very eve of the war, he made further personnel changes, replacing the head of the army counter-intelligence, Dimitrijevic, General Farkas. And so it was on the 23rd of March he declared an imminent threat of war which had in law as we've already seen the effect of subordinating the VJ -- the MUP to the VJ. And on the 24th of March, the FRY Prime Minister who had made the earlier declaration - not the President - declared a state of war. The Prosecution's submission is that by this time, the decision had been made pursuant to whatever earlier intentions or plan that the KLA would be annihilated and that as promised, there would be substantial depopulation of large parts of Kosovo of its Albanian population. On the eve of the heightened conflict, of what were the forces available to the accused comprised? Elements of the VJ's 3rd Army, the 52nd Corps, known as the Pristina Corps, several brigades, and also -- these are VJ soldiers that we're looking at. In addition, there were the police forces taking part. I said earlier we'd just show you what police forces looked like. This is just one picture of many. They were, of course, armed units that to the uninitiated would look probably like an army. And we'll see more pictures, then, in the course of the trial. They're equipped with APCs, mortars, heavy machine-guns, having special units with yet more powerful weaponry. The totality of units, I think, includes military terrorist units, civil defence units, reserve MUP units, as well as the armed Serb civilians, all organised at the municipality level where necessary falling within official chains of command. Can we look, please, at Exhibits 19 and 20. Yes. Your Honour, there is one very simple point that I desire to make in relation to the matters that are going to be dealt with by Mr. Ryneveld. And it can be dealt with by this map. I've got a larger version of it. I don't know if it shows up on the screen or if you've got a copy of it at hand. We have a larger version, but I'll have to try and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm concerned really. I don't know whether if we look at the -- if -- see if the camera can focus on this and if it's any better than the small version on the ELMO. I don't know if that can be done. See if it's preferable. It may be. Perhaps I can try it, and we'll see. And if it doesn't work, the AV unit tell me. Thanks very much. And I'll go back to the small version, which is a little bit too condensed. A couple of things. The indictment in this case breaks the events that were to follow down into deportation matters and killing matters. That's really a breakdown that's for the purposes of the indictment rather than necessarily reflecting any distinction of activities on the ground. So when we see references to deportation sites and reference to killing sites, it's not to say that they are entirely separable events. They're obviously integrated. But that's the way it's been done. As the -- as the Court will know, the Prosecution's case is that so far as Kosovo is concerned, the principal objective may have been or was deportation, removal of the population, to be achieved by whatever means were necessary, and killing was, of course, one of them. Killing people, you frighten the others into going. The map that you have before you deals with the sites where deportation is the principal apparent objective of those committing offences, and the sites that appear as deportation sites thus in the indictment. As I say, there's always an overlap and in nearly all deportation sites there were killings. However, we see here the sites with the dates on them of when the deportation activity started. Starting at the top, 25th of March, 29th of March; going around to Pristina, 24th of March; going down little further, 24th of March; coming across, 25th of March, 27th of March; going down, 24th, 25th of March; and then further down, 25th of March again. Can there be any doubt from that simple coincidence of dates but that what was happening was an overall and planned deportation and nothing else? That's assuming the Chamber finds the evidence supports deportation starting at those sites on those days. This map also shows, with the little red marks at the borders, the places through which people were deported. The killing sites map, which is the other document you have - and I'll put that up as well - shows a similar story. 26th of March at the top, with other -- 24th of March at the bottom, 26th of March here, 25th of March at Prizren, 25th of March further up at Djakovica, 26th of March just above that. And as I say, there is, in any event, a greater integration of killing sites and deportation sites than the indictment itself might suggest, the indictment, of course, also being constrained by the inability to put everything in and having to be selective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So as far as the sites are concerned, presumably we can look at both types of site under the same heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we need to be looking at the sites, rather than the particular categories which they pertain to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And indeed -- absolutely so, Your Honour. Indeed in most deportation sites there will be killings as well, the significance of which it may be all too obvious that the killing itself was part of the pre-plan. The question arises: Was it just a natural incident of forces sent to deport people that they will kill, or is it something that they do because it was required of them? And then one other part and one other point only -- because the case can in a sense be dealt with in the most elementary way quite properly in looking for the underlying intent of what was being -- what was being done. The significance of the fact that everybody had their identification papers taken away at the border, is that accidental or intentional? If it was being done intentionally, was it a plan? What had that plan got to do with NATO, as the accused would ask you to believe. So with those merely prefatory remarks, I'll turn from the crime base which -- I may make one or two observations in the course of what's left of my address, but I'll leave the rest of that to Mr. Ryneveld. But the case is extremely simple. Of course the accused got away with so much in the past maybe, but he thought he could get away with this. We say, looking at it as it were from the top still, when you see all the connections that can be established both in law and in fact, what was being done was a coordinated effort by leaders of the republic and of Serbia with their forces acting in concert. These were actions similar in nature to what had happened in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina where Serbian military and paramilitary forces had forcibly expelled and deported non-Serbs from areas under Serbian control. The evidence and an expert analysis of it in due course will show that the army and the MUP operations correlate strongly with -- as between deportations and killings. I've dealt with that already and why it isn't just a coincidence. It's part of a plan. The operations by the republic and by Serbian armed forces happened in responsibility -- in the areas of responsibility of different army brigades, different MUP stations, different zones of local administration in a coordinated way. And such an operation involving several different organisations under the threat of NATO bombing required a high level of planning. Because in the midst of actions against the KLA and against NATO, the narrow roads of Kosovo ended up being clogged with the refugees that the accused wanted to exclude from their homeland. We say that this is not a case of renegade local groups or anything like that. The scale of the operations and the consistency exclude that as a possibility. And you'll hear evidence directly of coordination of the army and the MUP paramilitaries and other units, all of which answered to this accused. Again, I don't want to trespass on the area that's going to be covered by Mr. Ryneveld, but you will hear area -- you will hear evidence in short that reveals an atmosphere of impunity for crimes being created, however brutal they may have been. As to the suggestion that Albanians moved out of areas of likely combat for their own good, we say the lie will be shown to that when you hear the detail of what in fact happened and of how it was that these people were driven out. And of course, being moved out for your own good is hardly consistent with having all the documents of identification or identification papers or your cards, documents taken away from you so that you have no identity once you've left. On the 24th of March, there was a discussion with Milosevic who said there was no problem with Kosovo. We'll hear a little more from Mr. Ryneveld about the significance of that conversation in due course. The ruthlessness of the accused's project emerges too from his callous attitude towards Serb victims during the NATO campaign. He said to one person enough -- that they needed enough civilian victims to turn the opinion of NATO countries against the bombing. So in our suggestion to the Chamber, this is a simple, in a sense, case to prove, and the Chamber should not in due course -- although it will explore all matters of importance with great care, we know, it shouldn't allow itself to be misled by the fog that may be created arising from the international negotiations, their twists and turns in which the accused took part, showed resistance, or handed matters over to others. That fog shouldn't be allowed to hide the reality that what happened on this occasion was the intentional, planned, criminal expulsion of his own people because of the attitude they took to him. Your Honour, just give me one minute. Matters ended this way: By June 1999, about 800.000 Kosovo Albanians, one third of the entire Kosovo Albanian population, had been expelled. Thousands more were believed to be internally displaced, and an unknown number had been killed. On the 3rd of June, the FRY and the Federal Republic of Serbia accepted a document of principles towards of resolution of the crisis which was presented to their representatives by Martti Ahtisaari on behalf of the European community and by Viktor Chernomyrdin for the President the Russian federation. That was followed by a Security Council resolution providing for a political solution to the Kosovo crisis, including an immediate end to violence and a rapid withdrawal of the republic's and Serbian's military police and paramilitary forces. There followed a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. military technical agreement. And what by way of post script to these particular events? Well, just this: Ojdanic, Pavkovic, Lazarevic, Vasiljevic were decorated, promoted by this accused. I have a few other supplementary points to make. I just want to check one thing with Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's been, of necessity, a rapid and abridged account of the accused's involvement over many years in three areas of conflict. Abridged though it has had to be, I hope we have revealed how there are going to be before you many lines of connection. Some connections in law under Constitutions and proper authority, many otherwise, that link him unavoidably to the events with which he is charged. There will be many strands of evidence, starting in Kosovo, ending in Kosovo, passing through the failures of, so far as he's concerned, of Croatia and Bosnia, all of which reveal a single continuing state of mind of his, transaction of his executed though it might have been, indeed was, through a small but changing and changeable cast of characters, and at the end of the day, what can be said to summarise the awful tragedies into which we must now shortly start to inquire? Croatia, Bosnia, and Kosovo shared in common that Serbia was either their neighbour indeed more than their neighbour, so far as Kosovo was concerned, and that the accused had a hand, a controlling hand, in their recent destinies. From the beginning, this accused has attempted to persuade those who would listen to him that what happened was inevitable. His powers of persuasion are considerable. I think I referred yesterday to the power and quality of that speech of his where he made a reference to the use of armed conflict in a speech that was otherwise apparently full of some good things. He was a man capable of persuading. He was a man capable of having others follow him. But as we look at what happened in the former Yugoslavia, things that happened weren't inevitable. They were not the acts of God but they were the acts of men. They were the results of decisions of men and significantly of this one, taken with no regard to the interests or even to the lives of others in a way that this Chamber may in due course find hard or impossible to comprehend. And in truth, it was having this accused, so far as Croatia and Bosnia was concerned, as a neighbour, and indeed so far as Kosovo was concern, having him as a neighbour that sealed so many fates. In a career spanning 13 years, and we will say a career -- a criminal career spanning at least eight years, it may be hard to express briefly those elements which were constant, but throughout that period, as the learned Prosecutor said in her opening remarks in perhaps slightly different words, he sought two things; to maximise his power and control, including territorial control by and of Serbs, to maximise control over Serbs. He did this by denying basic fundamental rights to those who disagreed with him. And, of course, in the brevity of my address, I've understated the wider elements of persecution that the Chamber will be familiar with from other cases and with which we will have to deal here, but he denied all sorts of rights, some that initially looked minor, progressing as they did ultimately to the denial of the right of non-Serbs to live among their neighbours or, indeed, to live at all. While he led his country, he always sought to assure them that they were not at war. Serbia was not at war. That the wars he caused were happening elsewhere, in other countries, not our own affair. Does the Chamber recall what I suggested was one of his mechanisms of control, of having things done by others over whom he had influence so that he could absolve himself of moral responsibility and thus explain why, for him, never regret, never shame. Well, he did the same thing with his people. "Nothing to do with us." But of course, the distinction upon which he relied for this part of his presentation in the world, the distinction of state from state, mattered not at all to him as indeed -- as was said at an early part of my address yesterday, attributable to him, he wasn't interested in borders but in only what was described, I think, as nations. The only border ultimately that he was interested in and that he did much to create, or to cement, was the border between Serb and non-Serb. He made a point of bringing conflict to the point where the army had to be used, but still Serbia wasn't at war but he was. He tells us that he was defending his people. They have not asked for his protection. They were not under attack. And Serbia today is again at peace, after many years, rebuilding many years of war, or wars of a kind, rebuilding its ties with its neighbours. I remind the Chamber of what the Prosecutor said about the need to look for individual and not for any kind of overall guilt. It's just the individual guilt of this person with whom we are concerned. And of course, what he did or tried to do was to make his people his unwitting accomplices who, once drawn into his plans, despite never voting on them, I dare venture to say could have no escape or no escape for a long time from the consequences of what he did. What he did at the time in laying plans for the future was, I dare say, that which often happens in crime. And war crimes are crimes. They are things people do, knowing that they are acting contrary to law and against the interests of humanity. What they do and what this accused did was to try and dissolve himself away from the picture of events that was developing. The trouble with all that is, that dissolve yourself away from the centre of events may leave a gap. There may be nobody else left to fill that gap, nobody else to whom you can point as being responsible for the events that are actually yours. All the events into which this Chamber will now have to inquire will, we submit, point towards a central personality, the existence of a controlling human force. It's a personality the accused seeks to say is not his, but there is no other. And we say when you've examined all the evidence, that the silhouette of that personality, indeed the full-face view of that personality at the centre of these events is unmistakably that of this accused. As with the other indictments, I don't need to review in detail the allegations that are contained in the public indictments. And now, if it's convenient to the Chamber, Mr. Ryneveld will deal with the crime base matters and the evidence relating to that, unless I can assist you further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honours. I would anticipate that I will be easily done before the end of the next session. I wonder whether you want me to start now and break it or would you rather take an early break and have me start then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I think if you start now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. If it please Your Honours, over a half a century ago, Mr. Justice Jackson, the Chief Prosecutor before the International Military Tribunal, opened the Nuremberg trial with these words: "The wrongs which we seek to condemn and punish have been so calculated, so malignant and so devastating that civilisation cannot tolerate their being ignored because it cannot survive their being repeated." He reflected on the grave responsibility imposed by opening the first trial in history for crimes against the peace of the world. At that time, the world hoped that the verdicts in that case would act as a deterrent to future war leaders by having sent a clear message that war crimes and crimes against humanity would be prosecuted according to the rule of law. They hoped that trials of that nature would never be necessary again. Unfortunately, that hope appears to be in vain. History appears to have repeated itself. The lessons, if learned at all, were either ignored or forgotten. The reign of terror perpetrated by Serb forces during the Milosevic regime in Kosovo has sadly necessitated that today will mark another historic legal first. With this trial, we start the first prosecution of a former sitting head of state of any nation for crimes committed while in office. And it is, accordingly, an equally grave responsibility to be involved in a trial holding Mr. Milosevic accountable according to the rule of law for the allegations of deportations, forcible transfer, murders and persecution with which he stands charged in the indictment now before you. The Prosecutor of the ICTY, Carla Del Ponte, has given her introductory remarks, and my colleague Mr. Nice has already outlined for you an overview of the Prosecution's case with respect to all three indictments which have now been joined as one trial. He has also outlined how we intend to prove that Mr. Milosevic is legally responsible and criminally accountable for the acts and omissions of the Serb forces who committed these atrocities. As the senior trial attorney responsible for the Kosovo component of this trial, it is now my duty to outline for you on the balance of the Prosecution's opening statement the nature and scope of what we will refer to as the crime base evidence for Kosovo. In so doing, I hope to give you a thumbnail sketch of what happened during roughly the first six months of 1999. This overview is intended to provide the Trial Chamber with a framework of the Kosovo case. Your Honours, it is the Prosecution's submission that the trial before you today is primarily a deportation case. You will hear from witnesses and read in reports and statements that by June of 1999, over 800.000 Kosovo Albanian civilians had been forced from their homes by Serb forces and had to flee to neighbouring states. Now, when I say "Serb forces," I'm talking about the forces of the FRY; Yugoslavia, the republic; and of course the MUP; the police; and certain paramilitary groups. For ease of reference, we'll refer to them as Serb forces. You will see before you on the screen again a map of the Balkans that my learned colleague Mr. Nice also showed. In the process of the 800.000 or so Serbs being forced from their homes, thousands of civilians were murdered. Many of the victims included the elderly as well as women and children. Now, before I go any further, it must be said that there was an armed conflict ongoing in Kosovo between the FRY and Serb forces, on the one hand, and the Kosovo liberation army, or KLA, on the other hand. Further, it must be said that in terms of armed conflict, it is an unfortunate, disturbing, but inescapable fact that people are killed. Undoubtedly, during this particular armed conflict, certain armed combatants from both sides of the conflict were killed as legitimate casualties of war. The fact that people die during times of war does not necessarily signify that a war crime has been committed. That having been said, it must be stressed that is not what this case is about. This case is about persecution in many forms, of civilians on a widespread and systematic scale. These acts, when perpetrated against civilian non-combatants, become war crimes and shall be prosecuted pursuant to the jurisdiction of this Honourable Tribunal. Although the indictment covers the period of the 1st of January, 1999, until the 20th of June, 1999, it must be remembered that the discriminatory campaign of persecution and expulsion directed at Kosovo Albanians started much earlier. In our pre-trial brief, we point to the fact that during certain periods of 1998, similar campaigns had already resulted in the internal displacement of thousands of refugees. According to UNHCR data which will be introduced at trial, by the end of October 1998, some 285.000 Kosovars had already been internally displaced. This campaign of persecution and expulsion increased in intensity and ferocity towards the end of March 1999, at about the same time that the international monitors were withdrawing from Kosovo. UNHCR staff nevertheless continued to monitor the number of refugees crossing at border points throughout Kosovo. Now, their data reflects that by the 30th of March, about 94.000 Kosovars, most of whom were women, children, and older people, had fled Kosovo since the 24th of March, 1999. So we're talking about a one-week period. Many reported deliberate expulsions and destruction of their homes, and many of them didn't know the whereabouts of their men, having been separated from them at the time of the expulsion. You will hear about cumulative daily totals of refugees counted by UNHCR officials. Those reports will show not only the daily tallies of refugees but will also show that these people reported being forced to leave their homes in freezing temperatures, at night, on foot, some barefoot. Thousands arrived by bus and train, having been gathered together by Serb authorities, awaiting expulsion. The report goes on to describe that tens of thousands were on the move inside Kosovo during weather described as freezing and rainy winter conditions and that several children were reported to have died of dehydration. Finally, this report will indicate that, according to UNHCR figures, an estimated 860.000 Kosovars left Kosovo between the 24th of March, 1999, and the 10th of June, 1999. Now, that is what we mean when we say that this case is primarily a deportation case. Undoubtedly, at some time during the course of this trial the suggestion will be made by Mr. Milosevic, or others on his behalf, that the reason these people fled Kosovo was because of the NATO bombing and not because of Serb forces attacks. I want to address that matter right up front during this opening. It is the Prosecution's submission that the witnesses will tell you that the vast majority of refugees fled their homes because of the attacks by Serb forces and not because of NATO bombing. You will also have the benefit of expert report prepared by Dr. Patrick Ball. This report analyses the data obtained from sources, including the UNHCR, about refugee movements during the relevant period. In essence, the independent assessment in this report, if accepted by the Tribunal, will corroborate the other evidence. Significantly, the analysis suggests that the effects of KLA and NATO activity are inconsistent with the observed patterns of refugee flow and killings. This report, we anticipate, will corroborate what nearly every single witness will tell you; they left because of fear and terror of the advancing Serb troops and not because of NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, what if the Chamber were to find as a matter of fact that they fled because of NATO bombing? Will you be addressing that, the legal position there?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I certainly will later in the address, if I may. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: From the body of evidence you will hear during the course of this trial, it will become patently obvious that the massive refugee movement throughout Kosovo was a direct consequence of the Serb forces. You see, they executed a concerted plan to terrorise the ethnic Albanians into leaving. Villagers would hear the sound of artillery from neighbouring villages, see the houses burning, hear horror stories from the fleeing victims and feared that the same fate awaited them. Consequently, many of them would load their families on carts or tractors or any means of transport available and join the convoy to avoid being beaten, raped, or murdered. The killings, lootings, rapes, and destruction of property were specifically designed to terrorise the population into leaving. It will also become apparent that the architects of this ethnic cleansing campaign took advantage of the onset of NATO bombing to intensify their actions. You will note from the evidence that during the week of the 24th to the 30th of March, Serb forces went on a major killing and deportation spree, intending to blame the deaths and refugee convoys on NATO bombing. The withdrawal of the KVM monitors in anticipation of bombing and the onset of NATO activities gave the Serb forces the perfect opportunity to escalate their campaign and put the blame on others, and that, you will conclude from the evidence, we would submit, is exactly what they did. You will hear evidence of mass executions and the systematic process by which Serb forces went from hamlet to hamlet, village to village, town to town murdering, raping, burning, looting, and destroying property in their path. On the monitor now you will see two photographs, which aren't coming through very clearly. Perhaps if we do them separately. The first photograph. There we are. The first photograph shows -- you can see a burning house with two soldiers standing in front with the three fingers raised. Another photo shows three different soldiers standing again in front of a burning house. This process had the intended effect of frightening the civilian population to leave their homes, their villages, and ultimately their province. The looting and burning had the desired consequence of ensuring that there was nothing for them to return to. You've heard reference to the burning of identification documents. As you can see from the photo now on the ELMO, we see bits burned passports and identification documents. That was typical of what occurred during this expulsion campaign. In many instances, their attackers told them to leave Kosovo and to go to Albania. You will hear that the Serb forces consistently robbed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the refugees of their identity documents and their vehicle licence plates. In so doing, they in essence removed all physical evidence that these people had citizen status and prevented them from claiming their legitimate and legal property rights should they attempt to return. All this was done to ensure that they ethnically cleansed the Kosovo Albanians from that province. It will become obvious from the evidence you will hear during the course of this trial that this campaign of deportation and ethnic cleansing occurred throughout Kosovo. The indictment before you, at least with respect to Kosovo, lists some 13 deportation sites and 12 killing or murder sites, some of which overlap. These locations are by no means the only sites where deportations or murders occurred. They are only a representative sample of what actually occurred throughout Kosovo. Before I turn to a discussion of some of the details of the deportation and killing sites contained in the indictment, it may be of some assistance to the Trial Chamber to refer to the maps of Kosovo depicting those sites. Some of them were already shown by Mr. Nice, with some dates on them. These show -- the first map we now have is the deportation map. You will note that the blue dots representing the villages or towns that will be discussed in the evidence during the course of this trial are not isolated to only one geographical area. Indeed, they cover practically the entire province of Kosovo. This map demonstrates the widespread and systematic nature of the deportation scheme. When one considers that most of these locations were ethnically cleansed in one week, between the 24th of March and the 31st of March, it becomes obvious that there was a wholesale and concerted effort by the Serb forces to round up and deport as many Kosovo Albanians as possible in a short time span. The irresistible inference to be drawn from this fact is that this did not occur by happenstance. This was not merely the result of a confluence of coincidences. The evidence you are about to hear will clearly show that this was the result of the coordinated attack by various Serb forces; the Yugoslav army or VJ, and the police or MUP, acting in concert. The pattern repeats itself from village to village. This was a planned and deliberate modus operandi on the part of the combined Serb forces carried out throughout Kosovo. That shall become absolutely crystal clear when you hear the evidence. I am about to turn to the killing site map. Is this an appropriate moment?
